rv.q: The Roundabout revival is so blissfully staged and packs such a delightful comic punch, it made me retroactively regret missing the last Kiss Me, Kate mounting, which ran on Broadway from 1999 to 2001 and starred the late, great Marin Mazzie opposite Brian Stokes Mitchell.

Spring was tardy this year, so if you are still suffering from seasonal affective disorder, you might try some therapeutic theater courtesy of the radiant revival of “Kiss Me, Kate,” which is spreading high-summer sunshine at Studio 54.
This revival of 'Kiss Me, Kate' is so much fun that you may well find yourself grinning from ear to ear before the first act is half over.
In Bartlett Sher’s plushly enjoyable staging, it delivers glorious music and falderol frivolity.

This handsome, well-cast revival of Cole Porter's 1948 musical comedy proves that Kiss Me, Kate still has plenty of bite. Kelli O'Hara and Will Chase make a formidable pair as the divorced actors whose onstage chemistry in The Taming of the Shrew mirrors their offstage tensions.
The design, like much else in this Kiss Me, Kate, keeps perfectly true to the fashions of Cole Porter having a blast with William Shakespeare.
I've seen funnier, freer revivals of 'Kiss Me, Kate,' mostly staged in more amusing or anarchic times; the revival's weakness, I think, is a lack of comfort with improvisational possibility.
For me, the adjustments, especially Ms. Green’s and Ms. O’Hara’s, are completely successful.
The gender-flipped revival of 'Kiss Me, Kate'

"Even in an imperfectly cast revival like the new Roundabout production, it's virtually impossible not to surrender to its boisterous charms...If the changes dampen some of the show's comedic vitality in order to make it palatable to contemporary sensibilities, so be it. There are corresponding losses and gains, too, in O'Hara's performance...

The clever navigation of this Golden Age musical through today's waters of gender politics is one of several plusses in an otherwise uneven production that is still able to score some highs in terrific dancing, Kelli O'Hara's performance and, oh, those Porter songs.
An uneven but still enjoyable revival that scores some highs in terrific dancing, Kelli O'Hara's performance and Porter songs.
Director Scott Ellis lets O'Hara and Chase and the rest of the cast win the audience over with the glorious music.
The sad truth — sad at least for a longtime lover of Porter’s songs — is that for all its pizzazz, Kiss Me, Kate itself feels irretrievably dated.
While the leads sparkle and Ellis's production showcases the jazzy score, it's an otherwise sedate affair.
This 'Kiss Me, Kate' should make even the grumpiest audience member fall in love with the power of great musical theater.
O’Hara deserves a thousand kisses along with our eternal worship for gracing us with two and a half glorious hours in this altogether wunderbar production.
This new "Kiss Me, Kate" is a joy.

Roundabout’s smartly-tweaked presentation of Kiss Me, Kate gives new life to an undeniable Broadway classic, while subtly reminding us of the progress women have made, since Shakespeare’s time and the 1940s.
This is a jaunty piece of theatre that aims no higher than your heart and scores a direct hit.
To quote the title tune, this Kate is absolutely bellisimo.

"A snappy, scintillating, and decidedly woke new production at Studio 54 and featuring an altogether smashing cast headed up by Kelli O'Hara (never better!) and Will Chase...Even if you are a Porter or Shakespeare purist, if you leave your high horse in the stable and join the crowd, you will have a wonderful time.
Cole Porter’s 1948 masterpiece of dramatic romance and ribald sass is still “Wunderbar!” over 70 years later.
Porter’s wit still shines through in his score.
Terrifically performed and staged as this revival is, the kids are more than likely to now see that there is indeed something quite "wunderbar" about this show.
This Kiss Me Kate is a show that knows exactly what it wants to be and achieves it with abundant style, wit, and most important of all, joy.
Gone is the shiny schmaltz of the Golden Age musical’s previous productions, Ellis instead grounding the piece, when necessarily, in sincerity and reality.

What’s on stage at Studio 54 works—because how could it not, when you have a company headlined by O’Hara and Chase singing such Porter gems as “Another Op’nin’, Another Show,” “So in Love,” and “Wunderbar”?
More spirited than exciting, this brisk revival looks nice, sounds pretty, moves fleetly, and rarely ceases to beguile the eye and ear.
It's so damned entertaining, joyously staged and performed that the minor politically correct tweaks to its book hardly matter.
This Kiss Me, Kate is a real treat.
O’Hara’s wry retreat with Chase is much more sophisticated.
Whether she’s hitting high notes or swatting her male co-star, Kelli O’Hara — funny and fierce — is reason enough to see “Kiss Me, Kate.”
They are both spirited, independent women not finally afforded independence, spiritual and otherwise.
O'Hara brings a subdued charm to the usually more boisterous part of Lilli, even if she is positively beaming when she first arrives on stage.
There are several fun numbers and pleasing bits in this Kiss Me Kate, although not as many as I would have liked.
But in Scott Ellis’s anemically directed production, neither has the staying power or depth to celebrate (or reimagine) the 1949. Tony Award-winning hit.
It’s a farce without spark or any real point of view.

These textual changes (although puzzling) are not necessarily detrimental, but they reveal the extent to which Roundabout is unsure of how to produce or interpret “Kiss Me, Kate” today, which further lends to the feeling of it being an utterly pointless revival.
Worse, in my opinion, is that those coming to it for the first time won’t find much to fall in love with.
Kiss Me Kate is just that kinda show; one of the finest old musicals around.
It’s singing and dancing puts us gleefully, giddily back in Broadway’s Golden Age.
This Kiss Me Kate glides effortlessly through and around the problems, while preserving the energy and excitement of the original.
The result is more even-handed, less humiliating, and vaudevillian—and what remains is a fully enjoyable comedy of manners in the style of Noël Coward.

"For all the pleasures this revival offers, Ellis’ production comes with several serious caveats. Purists will find Green’s tweaking of the book more sore-thumby than the similar but smoother surgery Guare performed...
Here is Kate the vessel that even a clever reimagining can't fill.
I kept wondering why the show seemed flat overall despite so many enjoyable sections.

Some key casting mistakes keep this well-appointed production from soaring where it should, but the choreography is a knockout and the musical itself so structurally sound and well-written that it cannot fail to entertain—uneven as it is, but still satisfying.
What results from both is a lopsided production that lacks a certain finish and fullness.
Kiss Me Kateis one of my favorite musicals with a strong score and a timeless story, and though there is much to like here, the second act after “Too Darn Hot” seems to fall apart.

cn.t: Critics largely praise this lavish revival for Kelli O'Hara's luminous vocals and Warren Carlyle's dazzling choreography, though some find it lacks energy and others note the show's dated gender politics remain problematic despite minor updates.

sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Orchestra rows E-G as the best seats overall, citing 'a winning mix of perfect proximity and elevated view over the heads in front' on a good rake with a low stage. Headout notes the 'outstanding inclination' keeps sightlines clear from middle rows. AVFMS Row D seat 2: 'Perfect view with unlimited legroom.' 16-row section seats ~350 of the 413 total; low stage means front rows don't require neck strain.

SeatPlan explicitly names Left and Right Mezzanine as 'the best value seats at the Laura Pels Theatre,' citing cheap tickets vs. central Orchestra with 'a clear and close view.' Only 3 rows (AA/BB/CC), under 100 seats — feels intimate and close to stage. Headout confirms 'very little restriction from the Mezzanine overhang at the back' of the Orchestra, meaning the Mezzanine itself is close/low. Row BB flagged by Headout as a specific value row.
